title: Definition and purpose of Fail-Fast and Fail-Safe iterators

blocks.text: 8.5.1. Definition and Purpose of Fail-Fast and Fail-Safe Iterators

At 02:00 the renewal-reminder job stops with a `NullPointerException`. The one reminder it sent before stopping quoted Jane Doe a price of minus 560 dollars. The stack trace names the reminder job's methods and `main`. Both customers came in at 14:05 from a partner's CSV file, and nothing in the trace says so.

Unit 6.5.3 showed fail-fast in an `ArrayList` iterator, which usually throws at the next step after the list changes under it. More generally, a component handed something it can't work with throws at once, while the caller and the bad value are both on the stack. Fail-safe is the opposite choice: carry on with a substitute. Units 8.5.2 and 8.5.3 return to iterators, the weakly consistent kind and how to choose one. Every output is from Java 21.
A Null Stored Now Fails Later, in a Trace That Doesn't Name Who Stored It
The customer is a plain record, and the importer copies whatever the file holds:
public record Customer(String name, String email, int discountPercent) {}

The partner's file had a row for Jane Doe with discount `1500` (the partner meant 15.00 % and sent basis points), and a row for John Roe with no email column. The program imports both rows, then runs the job, where `sendAll` loops over the customers and `send` prints one reminder:

imported 2 customers
to jane@example.com: your plan renews at -56000 cents
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.strip()" because the return value of "Customer.email()" is null
	at Reminders.mailbox(Reminders.java:15)
	at Reminders.send(Reminders.java:11)
	at Reminders.sendAll(Reminders.java:7)
	at Main.main(Main.java:13)
Before reading on: which line would you fix?

Java 21's message names the null exactly, the return value of `Customer.email()`. It can't name where the null came from. A stack trace holds the frames that are on the stack when the exception is created, and the constructor that stored the null returned twelve hours earlier. To find it you search for every place that builds a `Customer`, and to find the row you need the partner's file, which by now may have been replaced by the next one. The loop has no catch, so the first bad customer also ends the run for every customer after it.

A discount of 1500 is a valid `int` and the arithmetic is valid, so for Jane's row nothing threw, and the reminder went out with a negative price. No later null check would have seen it: the value is present and wrong.
A Check in the Constructor Puts the Caller in the Trace
Every `Customer` is made by its constructor, so a check there runs while the code holding the bad value is still on the stack:
The same importer, run once with John's row and once with Jane's:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: email
	at java.base/java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.java:259)
	at Customer.<init>(Customer.java:7)
	at Importer.importRow(Importer.java:6)
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: discountPercent 1500 is not in 0..100
	at Customer.<init>(Customer.java:11)
	at Importer.importRow(Importer.java:6)
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)

The frame under the constructor is now the importer, at 14:05, with the row in a local variable. The importer can catch the exception per row, report "row 2: email" to the partner while the file is still at hand, and store nothing the 02:00 job can trip on. A `Customer` with a discount of 1500 can no longer exist, so neither can the negative price.

`requireNonNull` accepts `""` and `" "`, which is what a file that has the column but leaves the cell empty gives you. A row whose email cell holds a space stops the same import with `IllegalArgumentException: email is blank`.

A check in the constructor holds only while the object can't change afterwards. `String` and `int` fields can't, but a `List` argument is still held by the caller, and `Collections.unmodifiableList` is a read-only view of the caller's list, not a copy:
view: [vip, null], copy: [vip]

`List.copyOf` returns an unmodifiable list that doesn't follow the caller's, and it throws `NullPointerException` if the list holds a null, so one call checks the elements and keeps them checked. A record with a `List<String> tags` component stores `List.copyOf(tags)`.
An Assertion Checks Nothing Unless the JVM Runs with -ea
The range check written as an assertion:

$ java Asserts
Customer[name=Jane Doe, email=jane@example.com, discountPercent=1500]
$ java -ea Asserts
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.AssertionError: discountPercent 1500
	at Asserts$Customer.<init>(Asserts.java:4)
	at Asserts.main(Asserts.java:9)

Maven's Surefire plugin enables assertions for tests by default, so this check fails the right test and is absent from a production JVM started without `-ea`. A value that comes from outside the class gets an `if` and an exception.

A Default Belongs Where Refusing to Start Costs More Than the Default

Fail-fast applied to configuration says a service with a setting missing should not start. The payment client reads three settings at startup. `gateway.url` has no safe value; `http.timeout.ms` and `retries` do, and `retries` is new in this release. Two loaders, where `required(file, key)` throws when the key is absent:
Both read the config file written for the last release, which has no `retries` line:

gateway.url=https://pay.example.com
http.timeout.ms=2000

strict  last release: refused to start: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing setting retries
lenient last release: Settings[gatewayUrl=https://pay.example.com, timeoutMs=2000, retries=2]

With the strict loader, the upgrade is also a config migration: every environment's file must gain the new line before the new version starts, and each instance whose file was missed stays down. Running with two retries, a value nobody had to choose, costs less than an instance that doesn't come up.
`gateway.url` stays required in both loaders. Any URL the code could fall back to would send payments somewhere they shouldn't go, so a missing one must stop the start.
A Default Also Hides a Misspelt Key, Unless Unknown Keys Stop the Start
During an incident the gateway answers slowly, and the on-call engineer edits the file so callers give up after 800 ms instead of 2 s, then restarts:

gateway.url=https://pay.example.com
http.timout.ms=800
lenient incident:     Settings[gatewayUrl=https://pay.example.com, timeoutMs=5000, retries=2]
Spot the problem before reading on.

`timout` is missing an `e`. `getProperty("http.timeout.ms", "5000")` finds no such key and returns the default, so the service restarts cleanly and now waits up to 5 s per attempt, longer than before the edit. Request threads pile up behind the gateway while the engineer believes the fix is live.
This loader keeps its defaults and refuses every key it doesn't know:

load    last release: Settings[gatewayUrl=https://pay.example.com, timeoutMs=2000, retries=2]
load    incident:     refused to start: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: unknown settings [http.timout.ms]

The last release's file still loads with the default, and the typo stops the restart with the key's name in the message. In a rolling restart that halts on a failed start, the first instance fails and the others keep serving. Logging a warning and carrying on would still run with 5,000 ms.

A value that doesn't parse is already a failure: `http.timeout.ms=800ms` stops `lenient` and `load` with `NumberFormatException: For input string: "800ms"`. A loader that catches it and uses the default would turn that failure back into the silent 5 s.

The rule has a cost too. Once a release refuses unknown keys, rolling back to it with a newer release's file fails: a loader that never heard of a key the newer file sets refuses to start. Old versions must either know the keys newer ones may write or tolerate them.

Summary

items: **A null stored now fails later, in a trace that doesn't name who stored it.** Java 21's message names the null, not the code that stored it, and an out-of-range value doesn't fail at all.
**A check in the constructor puts the caller in the trace.** Check null, blank and range with an `if`, not `assert`, and copy what the caller could still change.
**A default belongs where refusing to start costs more than the default.** A new optional key gets one; a key with no safe value stays required.
**A default also hides a misspelt key.** Refusing unknown keys keeps the default for absent keys and turns a typo into a failed start.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The partner sends 40,000 rows a night, and a dozen have no email. Do you refuse the file, refuse the rows, or store them flagged? What must the reminder job know in each case?
Settings come from environment variables instead of a file. How do you catch a misspelt variable name when the environment holds hundreds of names your service doesn't own?
Two services share one config file, each knowing half its keys. What becomes of refusing unknown keys, and what would you change?
Find a `requireNonNullElse` or `getOrDefault` in code you know. Is it a fail-safe default, or does it hide a bug?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Check Goes Where the Object Is Made

A check could sit in each method that uses a field, or once in the constructor. In the methods, every new method has to remember it, and the failure still comes late. In the constructor, the type itself carries the guarantee: every `Customer` that exists has an email and a discount between 0 and 100, and the code that uses one checks nothing. The cost is that every way of building one pays the check, including a test that wants a half-filled object. Data that was accepted under older rules, such as an old row with no email, can't be loaded at all until someone decides what it means, and the constructor forces that decision at import time rather than at 02:00.
